summary: Psalm 127 begins by saying that building, guarding, and exhausting work are vain unless Yahweh gives the outcome. It then turns to children, describing them as Yahweh’s heritage and as strength for a household when facing enemies in the gate.
whyItMatters: This psalm belongs among the Songs of Ascents and gives a compact wisdom reflection on dependence on God. It holds ordinary concerns together: homes, cities, work, sleep, children, and public vulnerability.

context.author: The heading says, “A Song of Ascents. By Solomon.” In Psalms, headings are ancient parts of the received collection, but their exact force can be debated; “By Solomon” may be read as authorship or association.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and instruction.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 127 is uncertain.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the Songs of Ascents, a group whose heading links them with ascent or pilgrimage language.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry and wisdom reflection, using parallel lines and vivid images rather than extended argument.

outline.heading: Work Without Yahweh
outline.note: Building a house and guarding a city are portrayed as empty labor if Yahweh is not the one who secures them.

outline.heading: Rest Against Anxious Toil
outline.note: The psalm challenges early rising, late nights, and “the bread of toil,” contrasting them with the sleep God gives to loved ones.

outline.heading: Children As Gift
outline.note: Children are described as a heritage and reward from Yahweh.

outline.heading: Children As Strength
outline.note: Children of youth are compared to arrows in the hand of a mighty man.

outline.heading: A Full Quiver At The Gate
outline.note: The psalm ends with the image of a man whose many children strengthen him when speaking with enemies in the gate.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. By Solomon. Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.
keyVerses.why: This opening states the psalm’s main claim: human work and vigilance matter, but they do not finally secure the house or city apart from Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.
keyVerses.why: The verse brings the same point into daily labor and rest, warning that anxious overwork cannot replace what God gives.

keyVerses.text: Behold, children are a heritage of Yahweh. The fruit of the womb is his reward.
keyVerses.why: This marks the psalm’s turn from building and guarding to family, naming children as a gift rather than simply a human achievement.

keyVerses.text: Happy is the man who has his quiver full of them. They won’t be disappointed when they speak with their enemies in the gate.
keyVerses.why: The final verse completes the arrow image and shows why the psalm sees children as public strength, not only private blessing.

questions.question: What does “A Song of Ascents” mean here?
questions.answer: The heading places this psalm among the Songs of Ascents. Headings can name genres, collections, performers, tunes, or other associations, and their exact historical force is not always recoverable. Here it identifies the psalm’s collection without giving a full setting inside the poem itself.

questions.question: Does “By Solomon” prove Solomon wrote the psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says “By Solomon,” but such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging. Readers differ on how strongly to take this as a byline. The safest statement is that the received heading connects the psalm with Solomon, while the psalm itself focuses on dependence on Yahweh in house, city, work, and family.

questions.question: What does “vain” mean in this psalm?
questions.answer: “Vain” appears in verses 1 and 2 to describe labor, guarding, and anxious toil that cannot secure their goal apart from Yahweh. The psalm is not saying building, watching, or working are worthless in themselves. It says their success is not finally controlled by human effort alone.

questions.question: Is the psalm against hard work?
questions.answer: No. The psalm mentions builders, a watchman, and people rising early and staying up late, so it knows ordinary labor and vigilance are part of life. Its warning is about treating labor as self-sufficient, as though enough effort could replace Yahweh’s giving and guarding.

questions.question: Why does verse 2 connect work with sleep?
questions.answer: Verse 2 contrasts exhausting toil with the statement that God “gives sleep to his loved ones.” The point is not that loved ones never work or never suffer sleeplessness. In the poem’s argument, sleep becomes a sign that life is received from God rather than secured by anxious labor alone.

questions.question: Does the psalm say people without children are less favored by God?
questions.answer: The psalm praises children as a heritage and reward, but it does not discuss every family situation or explain why some people do not have children. Readers should not turn this short poem into a complete doctrine of worth or divine favor. Its direct claim is positive: children are received as Yahweh’s gift.

questions.question: Why compare children to arrows?
questions.answer: Verse 4 compares “the children of youth” to arrows in the hand of a mighty man. The image emphasizes strength, reach, and readiness in a dangerous social world. Verse 5 develops the image with a full quiver and a scene involving enemies in the gate.

questions.question: What is “the gate” in verse 5?
questions.answer: The verse pictures a public place where a man speaks with his enemies. The psalm does not explain the exact setting beyond that scene. The main point is that a household with many children is portrayed as less exposed when conflict becomes public.

questions.question: How do the house, city, and children belong together?
questions.answer: The psalm moves from a house being built, to a city being watched, to a household strengthened by children. These are not separate topics dropped at random; together they describe forms of human security. In each case, the psalm directs the reader away from self-reliance and toward Yahweh as giver and protector.

glossary.def: In verse 1, the thing being built; within the psalm’s movement it can suggest ordinary household life and security, not just a physical structure.
The person who guards the city in verse 1; the psalm says even this vigilance is vain unless Yahweh watches over the city.
The phrase in verse 2 for life sustained by exhausting labor and anxious effort.
What verse 3 calls children: something received from Yahweh rather than merely produced by human planning.
The container for arrows in verse 5; the psalm uses it as an image for many children who strengthen a man in public conflict.
